The device stood in Egyptian temples, dispensing holy water for ritual washing to anyone who paid a coin for it, which suited priests who wanted a fair, unattended way to ration a scarce resource among pilgrims. It is the earliest known coin-operated machine, roughly two thousand years ahead of the vending machines it is compared to.

A farmer digging in a walled field on Milos in April 1820 uncovered the statue in two pieces. A French naval officer with an interest in antiquity, Olivier Voutier, was on the island and urged him to keep clearing the ground rather than stop at the first find.

A marble hand holding an apple turned up nearby and, by most reconstructions, belonged to the same figure, suggesting she once held the fruit in one hand while the other steadied her slipping drapery. French diplomats bought the statue before rival buyers could secure it, and Louis XVIII had it placed in the Louvre in 1821, arms already missing.

For over a thousand years, European anatomy had rested on Galen, who had dissected pigs and apes rather than people and assumed the results carried across. Vesalius opened human cadavers himself in 1543 and found Galen wrong on basics: the jaw is one bone, not two, and the breastbone has three parts, not seven.

His seven-volume Fabrica, printed in Basel, paired those corrections with roughly 273 plates showing flayed figures posed against landscapes, their skin and muscle peeled back layer by layer. Who drew them is still argued over, with a pupil of Titian's the leading but unproven candidate. Vesalius insisted the point was the dissecting, not the drawing.

JVC put its Victor HR-3300 recorder on sale in Japan on 9 September 1976, a year after Sony had already launched Betamax, entering a format war JVC had no obvious right to win. Sony's format offered comparable picture quality, but its cassettes held only an hour of recording, a limit that mattered to households buying a machine to tape a football match or a film.

VHS ran a slightly slower tape speed and simply fit more onto a longer cassette, giving it two hours from the start. JVC also licensed the format to any manufacturer willing to build for it, so Matsushita, Hitachi, Sharp and others backed VHS while Sony kept Betamax to itself, and by 1980 VHS held roughly 60 percent of the North American market.

The sagas credit Leif Erikson with the voyage, sailing after Bjarni Herjolfsson had already sighted an unknown coast without landing on it. The only confirmed Norse site in the Americas is L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, found in the 1960s by Anne Stine and Helge Ingstad, with a cloak pin, iron working debris and boat repair tools among its finds.

Tree rings from timber felled at the site let researchers date the Norse presence there with unusual precision. It was not a colony meant to last: the buildings suited an overwintering base and ship repair station, housing at most a few dozen people rather than a permanent settlement.

Viking 1 was meant to land on 4 July 1976, timed for the American bicentennial, until images of the planned site showed ground too rough to risk. NASA held the lander in orbit while it scouted a safer spot in Chryse Planitia, touching down on 20 July instead, seven years to the day after Apollo 11 reached the Moon.

The first photograph reached Earth 25 seconds after landing, showing rocks and a haze of dust the descent engines had kicked up. A colour image followed the next day, and the lander kept transmitting from the Martian surface for roughly six years, far longer than its planned mission.

Erik the Red was not exploring by choice. Outlawed from Iceland for killing a neighbour's kinsman after a feud that began with a landslide, he spent his three years of banishment charting the coast of an unknown land to the west, returning to Iceland once the exile ended.

He called it Greenland, by his own account because a good name would draw settlers a truer description would not. It worked: in 985 he led a fleet of colonists back across, and the settlements they founded on Greenland's southwestern coast lasted for centuries before eventually failing.

Medieval Icelandic sources credit Ingolfur Arnarson as the first settler who sailed to Iceland meaning to stay, landing around 874. Archaeology broadly backs the tradition: a layer of volcanic ash datable to the same years sits right beneath the earliest signs of turf houses and grazing across the island.

Settlement moved fast once it began. Landnamabok, the medieval book of settlements, names hundreds of families who claimed farmland along the coasts, and within a few decades the island was full enough that Icelanders founded the Althing, an assembly of free farmers, to settle disputes without a king.

Volta was answering a rival, not chasing an invention for its own sake. Luigi Galvani had argued that a frog's twitching leg proved animals carried their own electricity; Volta suspected the current came from the two different metals touching the tissue, not the tissue itself.

To prove it he stacked discs of copper and zinc, separated by cloth soaked in salt water, into a column that produced a steady current with no animal involved. He described the device, the voltaic pile, in a letter to the Royal Society in March 1800, and it became the first battery able to supply current continuously rather than in a single spark.

Voyager 1 left Earth on 5 September 1977, sixteen days after its twin Voyager 2, on a trajectory fast enough to overtake it and use Jupiter's and Saturn's gravity to fling itself toward interstellar space. Both probes carried a gold-plated record encoded with sounds and images of Earth, sequenced by a team led by Carl Sagan, in case anything ever intercepted one.

Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and remains the most distant human-made object, now more than 170 times the distance from Earth to the Sun and still returning data on radio signals that take over a day to arrive.

Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the sun's outward particle stream gives way to the galaxy's, on 25 August 2012, though nobody realised it at the time. The probe's plasma spectrometer had failed back in 1980, leaving scientists with no direct way to measure the density of charged particles around the spacecraft as it travelled.

Confirmation came from a solar eruption that reached the probe in April 2013 and set the surrounding plasma oscillating; from the frequency of those oscillations, researchers calculated an eighty-fold jump in electron density, the signature of interstellar rather than solar plasma. NASA did not announce the crossing until 12 September 2013, more than a year after Voyager 1 had actually left the solar wind behind.

In 1839, at a rubber works in Woburn, Massachusetts, Charles Goodyear dropped a mixture of rubber and sulphur onto a hot stove. Rather than melting further, it charred like leather, keeping its shape in cold weather and losing the stickiness that had doomed every earlier rubber product. He called the process vulcanisation.

The discovery never made him rich. Goodyear spent years defending the patent in court, was jailed for debt in both England and France, and died in 1860 owing roughly two hundred thousand dollars. Goodyear Tire and Rubber, founded decades after his death, only ever borrowed his name.

A limestone trackway across the Isthmus of Corinth, cut with parallel grooves to guide wheeled cradles, let the ancient Greeks haul entire ships between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf rather than sail the long, dangerous route around the Peloponnese. Built around 600 BCE, the Diolkos ran roughly six to eight kilometres, though only about a kilometre of paving has actually been excavated.

Merchants used it to move cargo, especially heavy stone and timber, while naval commanders shifted warships between seas in wartime, a manoeuvre recorded repeatedly between the fifth and first centuries BCE. It stayed in service for over six centuries, falling out of use by the mid first century CE, and its grooved track is the nearest ancient parallel to a railway.

No single inventor built the first electric washing machine. Alva Fisher is often named as the man behind it, and the Hurley Machine Company's early Thor model gets cited as the first, but the historical record does not support a clean claim of priority; newspapers were already advertising electric washers by 1904.

What changed around this period was not one patent but the wiring itself: as urban homes gained household electricity, manufacturers raced to fit motors to existing tub-and-wringer designs rather than invent the washing action from scratch. The motor did the turning; the labour it replaced, boiling and hand-wringing heavy wet linen, had barely changed in a century.

At Karnak's Precinct of Amun-Re, priests kept a stone vessel with sloping sides and a small hole near its base, marked inside with twelve columns of lines, one for each month. Water dripped out at a near-constant rate under Amenhotep III, and reading the falling level against the correct column gave the hour after dark, when a sundial was useless.

A tomb inscription credits an official named Amenemhet, roughly two centuries earlier, as the device's inventor, though none of his clocks has been found. The same principle, water draining at a measured rate, appears independently in Babylon, and both traditions used it chiefly for timing temple rituals and night watches, since the sun still told the hour well enough by day.

At Chemtou and Testour, in what is now Tunisia, Roman engineers built mills around the second century CE with a horizontal wheel of angled blades sunk fully underwater inside a circular cistern. Water entered at an angle, spinning as it dropped, so the wheel spun with the flow rather than merely being pushed by it, closer in principle to a modern turbine than to a simple paddle wheel.

The design let a mill run efficiently on a smaller, faster stream than the more familiar vertical waterwheel needed, useful in a hilly province without large steady rivers. Beyond grinding grain, the same submerged-wheel principle was later adapted in the empire for fulling cloth and sawing marble, work that depended on continuous, unattended power.

A shaft off the Israeli coast at Atlit-Yam, now under several metres of the Mediterranean, was dug by Neolithic villagers who lined it with stone as they went deeper, chasing a water table that dropped as they dug. It sits within a much larger submerged settlement, drowned when the sea rose after the last ice age.

Digging a well meant excavating below the point where a hole would simply collapse, which is why early examples are stone-lined shafts rather than open pits. The technique let settlements form away from rivers and springs, on ground chosen for farmland or defence rather than for standing water nearby.

Grinding grain came later. Water wheels first lifted water: paddle-driven lifting wheels appear in Egypt by the 4th century BC, built to move water into irrigation channels away from the Nile itself. Grinding came slightly later, with wheels turning millstones in the Near East by the 3rd century BC.

The design that survived best was the vertical watermill, which evolved in Syria and Asia Minor by around the 2nd century BC before spreading to Greece and the Roman world. From there it became one of the few sources of mechanical power available before steam, turning mills for centuries with no fuel but moving water.

King Sennacherib of Assyria had a stone aqueduct built near Jerwan, north of Nineveh, to carry water to his palace gardens, completed not long after 700 BCE from more than two million dressed stones. To stop the channel leaking across its arches, builders lined it with bitumen, natural tar seeping from nearby ground deposits, rather than a cement in the modern sense.

The finished structure stood roughly nine metres tall and stretched close to three hundred metres, carrying water across a valley on stone arches, a technique otherwise unrecorded until Roman aqueducts appeared centuries later. Some archaeologists count Jerwan as the oldest aqueduct of its kind anywhere, built five hundred years before Rome perfected the form.

Waymo One opened to the public in the Phoenix suburbs in December 2018, years after its parent project began as a secretive Google research effort. The earliest rides still carried a human safety driver behind the wheel, ready to take over, so the service was commercial before it was fully driverless in practice.

That changed in November 2019, when Waymo began running some Phoenix rides with no one in the driver's seat at all, the first company anywhere to do so. Rivals including Uber and Cruise had been racing toward the same milestone for years; Waymo's approach, built on a decade of accumulated mapping and sensor data around Phoenix's wide, predictable roads, got there first.

Travel was not what the wheel was first for. A potter's wheel from western Ukraine, dating to the middle of the fifth millennium BCE, predates any wheeled cart. Clay tablets from Uruk in Mesopotamia, showing wagons on wheels around 3500 to 3350 BCE, mark the first clear evidence of the wheel turned to moving people and goods rather than shaping clay.

The oldest wheel actually found in the ground, complete with its axle, was pulled from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia and dates to roughly 3130 BCE. Spoked wheels, light enough for fast chariots, did not appear until around 2000 BCE, invented far to the east by the Sintashta culture on the steppe.

A Han-dynasty tomb mural at Chengdu, dated to 118 AD, shows a man pushing a single-wheeled cart, the earliest firm evidence of the wheelbarrow anywhere. Unlike the design that later spread through Europe, the common Chinese version mounted its wheel in the centre of the frame rather than at the front.

That central placement carried the load's weight on the wheel itself rather than on the pusher's arms, so one person could shift loads far heavier than muscle alone allowed, and accounts describe versions capable of moving several passengers at once. It found steady work in construction, mining and farm transport across the centuries that followed.

The IEEE approved the 802.11 wireless networking standard in 1997, offering a maximum speed of just two megabits per second, too slow for most of what it would later be used for. It grew out of committee work that had begun years earlier to let devices share a radio spectrum band without licences or cables.

The name Wi-Fi came later, coined in 1999 by a branding firm hired by an industry alliance because 802.11 meant nothing to shoppers. Faster amendments, 802.11b and 802.11a, arrived within two years and made wireless networking practical for ordinary homes and offices rather than just laboratories.

Charles Brush built his turbine not on some remote hillside but in the garden of his own mansion on Euclid Avenue in Cleveland, a 12 kilowatt dynamo turned by a rotor that automatically adjusted itself to changing wind. It charged a bank of 12 batteries in his basement, making his house the first in Cleveland lit by electricity.

Brush was already wealthy from arc lighting and dynamo patents, so the turbine was as much a demonstration as a necessity. It kept his home continuously powered for 20 years without a single failure, a reliability record that took decades for later wind machines, built for the grid rather than one house, to match.

Sumerian physicians had nothing to numb a patient with beyond what was already on the table: fermented drink. Cuneiform medical tablets from Mesopotamia describe ethanol used to dull the senses before a procedure, alongside herbal mixtures, at a time when the alternative to any sedation at all was simply holding the patient down.

It was crude and unreliable next to what followed it. Sumerian texts from the same tradition also record the opium poppy in cultivation by around 3400 BCE, giving physicians a second, stronger sedative within a few centuries. Neither drug controlled dosage or pain with any precision, but both mark the first recorded attempts to manage it deliberately rather than not at all.

Charles Fenerty, a Nova Scotian in his early twenties, mailed a sheet of paper made from ground spruce to a Halifax newspaper on 26 October 1844 to prove wood pulp could replace cotton and linen rags. He had been testing the idea since his teens, unaware that a German inventor was chasing the same solution at the same time.

Friedrich Gottlob Keller patented a wood-pulp process in Germany the following year and sold rights to a papermaker who commercialised it, while Fenerty never patented his own. Cotton rag supply could not keep pace with rising demand for paper, and Keller is now the name most histories credit, despite Fenerty's earlier letter.

At Kalambo Falls in Zambia, two logs excavated beneath a waterfall bear notches cut to lock them together, deliberately shaped rather than simply broken or worn. Luminescence dating put the joint at around 476,000 years old, making it the oldest known wooden structure, built long before Homo sapiens existed, most likely by Homo heidelbergensis.

Wood decays far faster than stone, so the archaeological record of the Stone Age is overwhelmingly a record of what survived rather than what people actually used. Researcher Larry Barham has argued wooden tools were probably at least as common as stone ones throughout this period; Kalambo Falls, preserved only because the waterlogged ground starved the wood of oxygen, is the rare direct proof.

Tim Berners-Lee's problem at CERN in March 1989 was mundane: thousands of researchers came and went, and nobody could reliably find or share each other's documents across incompatible systems. His proposal called it a way of linking information without a central index, letting any file point to any other regardless of what computer held it.

By the end of 1990 he had built the pieces himself: a browser and editor called WorldWideWeb, the first web server, and the address and markup formats still in use. CERN released the technology to the wider internet in August 1991 and gave up all rights to it royalty-free in 1993, a decision that let it spread without licence fees.

A pair of rollers turning against each other can pull cotton fibre through while the seed, too large to pass, is stripped away behind it, and adding a worm gear let one crank handle drive both rollers at matched, opposing speeds instead of relying on two people working a simple hand crank each. The design belongs to the Delhi Sultanate, appearing somewhere in the thirteenth or fourteenth century on the Indian subcontinent.

Mughal workshops adopted the geared gin from around the sixteenth century, and the combination of worm gear and crank handle pushed Indian cotton textile output well beyond what earlier single-roller gins could manage. Versions of the same roller principle are still used in parts of the Indian subcontinent, largely unchanged from the medieval mechanism.

Caroline Murat, Napoleon's sister and Queen of Naples, ordered an oblong repeating watch from Abraham-Louis Breguet in 1810. It was paid for in 1811 and delivered in 1812, ultra-thin, fitted with a thermometer and mounted on a wristlet of hair braided with gold thread rather than a metal band.

Breguet catalogued it as N degrees 2639, describing it plainly as a repeater for the wrist. The piece itself has not survived, but the order books have, which is how its specifications are known at all. Pocket watches remained the norm for another century; the wristwatch caught on widely only once soldiers found fumbling for a chain watch impractical in the trenches.

Tim Berners-Lee had already built the web at CERN in 1989, largely to let physicists share documents across incompatible computers. On 6 August 1991 he posted a summary of the project to the alt.hypertext newsgroup and made the code freely available, with no patent and no licence fee attached.

That decision, more than the technology itself, is why the web spread rather than staying a lab tool. CERN's directors confirmed in 1993 that anyone could use the protocols royalty free. Within two years graphical browsers such as Mosaic turned Berners-Lee's text based system into something millions of non specialists could use.

Wilhelm Rontgen was testing whether cardboard could block emissions from a cathode ray tube in his Wurzburg laboratory in November 1895 when a screen across the room began to glow. Unsure what he had found, he called the unknown radiation X-rays, borrowing the mathematical symbol for something unidentified.

Six weeks later he photographed his wife Anna's hand, her bones and wedding ring visible through the flesh. She is said to have exclaimed that she had seen her own death. Rontgen refused to patent the discovery so it could spread freely into medicine, and in 1901 became the first person awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Xerox unveiled the 914 on live television from a New York hotel on 16 September 1959, a machine the size of a large desk that could copy a page in under seven seconds. The name came from its maximum paper size, nine by fourteen inches, and Xerox mostly rented rather than sold it, charging 25 dollars a month plus a small fee per copy rather than the 27,500 dollar purchase price.

The 914 had a real fault: documents dense with dark ink, especially rows of zeros, could scorch and occasionally catch fire, so every machine shipped with a small extinguisher that Xerox marketed cheerfully as a scorch eliminator. Ralph Nader later said his own office copier caught fire three times in four months. None of it slowed sales; by 1965 the 914 alone accounted for roughly two thirds of Xerox's revenue.

The maiden flight of LZ 1, on 2 July 1900 over Lake Constance, was not a triumph so much as a proof that the frame held together. Carrying five men, it climbed to 410 metres and covered six kilometres in seventeen minutes before an engine failed and a jammed weight forced it down.

Ferdinand von Zeppelin was in his sixties and had spent his own fortune on the project after the army turned it down. The rigid aluminium skeleton inside the fabric hull, rather than any single flight, was the idea that later airships and Germany's wartime fleet were built on.

Zhang Heng's bronze urn, built in 132 AD, ringed eight dragon heads around its rim, each facing a compass direction and holding a small ball in its jaws. A pendulum inside was tuned to tip toward the direction a distant tremor came from, tripping a lever that dropped that dragon's ball into the open mouth of a bronze toad below.

The Book of Later Han records one instance where the device dropped a ball toward the northwest while nobody in the capital felt anything. Skeptics at court dismissed it until a rider arrived days later reporting an earthquake in Longxi, in modern Gansu province, in exactly that direction.

The mines at Zawar, near Udaipur in Rajasthan, were already active under Mauryan rule, when the empire controlled most of the Indian subcontinent. Zinc ore is unusually stubborn: heated in an open furnace, the metal turns to vapour and simply escapes before it can be collected as a liquid.

Solving that took a sealed retort and a downward condenser, a technique Zawar's furnaces did not perfect until many centuries later, in the medieval period, when the site became the world's largest source of distilled zinc. The early mining nonetheless marks the start of a continuous industry on the same ground.

Whitcomb Judson called his device a clasp-locker, a mechanical hook-and-eye fastener meant to replace the tedious business of lacing a boot. He showed it at the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, where it drew little attention and even less enthusiasm, partly because the prototype jammed constantly.

The fastener people actually recognise today came from a different engineer, Gideon Sundback, who redesigned Judson's mechanism around 1913 with finer, more densely spaced teeth that interlocked far more reliably. It only earned its familiar name in 1923, when B.F. Goodrich fitted it to rubber boots and branded the sound of pulling it shut a zipper.
